title: Performance in Symmetry-Restricted Searches for Post-Quantum Correlations
abstract: Searches for post-quantum correlations depend on two distinct ingredients: how abundant such correlations are in the underlying correlation space and how efficiently the chosen representation preserves their distinguishability from quantum correlations. We quantify these effects by introducing the popularity rate and the projection acceptance, whose product defines the search performance. We illustrate these concepts in binary-outcome Bell scenarios with symmetry-related sites, using the CHSH and pyramid representations. Particular attention is paid to the distinction between exchange-symmetric synchronous correlations and correlations satisfying only exchange symmetry. In the synchronous quantum sector, the common-vector representation follows automatically from synchrony, whereas exchange symmetry alone defines a substantially larger correlation space. We show that this distinction can qualitatively change the effectiveness of a projected search: the pyramid representation, which retains substantial discriminatory power in the synchronous sector, has no discriminatory power when only exchange symmetry is imposed. Our results provide a simple framework for assessing and comparing searches for post-quantum correlations.
summary: This work develops a quantitative framework to measure how well one can search for correlations that violate quantum mechanics but obey no-signaling constraints. The performance metric combines the abundance of such correlations with how well a chosen mathematical projection preserves their distinguishability. A key finding is that relaxing symmetry assumptions can drastically reduce the effectiveness of the search, even if the underlying correlations still exist.
main_problem: The paper quantifies the performance of searches designed to detect post-quantum correlations (those correlations that violate quantum mechanics but are still consistent with no-signaling).
main_result: The effectiveness of these searches depends critically on the symmetry assumptions made; specifically, a projection useful for synchronous correlations loses all discriminatory power when only general exchange symmetry is imposed.
method: The performance is quantified by the product of the 'popularity rate' (abundance of post-quantum correlations) and the 'projection acceptance' (how much of that abundance survives a chosen mathematical projection).
model_or_system: The analysis uses bipartite Bell scenarios with binary outcomes, comparing correlations under strict synchrony versus those satisfying only exchange symmetry. The framework is generalized to $m$ measurement settings.
key_observables: Search Performance $S(\pi) = r \cdot A(\pi)$, Popularity Rate ($r$), Projection Acceptance ($A(\pi)$), and the CHSH value.
important_parameters: The number of settings per site ($m=2$ or $m=3$), and the specific symmetry constraints (synchronous vs. exchange).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on geometric volume fractions derived from the Lebesgue measure on the no-signaling reference space, and comparisons are made between outer approximations and exact quantum sets.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the distribution of post-quantum points in projected spaces (like the pyramid representation) for $m=3$, comparing accepted points against the boundaries of known correlation sets.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares the detection of post-quantum correlations under different symmetry assumptions (synchronous vs. exchange-symmetric) by calculating the search performance metric $S(\pi)$ for various projections ($\pi$).
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, quantitative framework for assessing the limitations of experimental tests for non-quantum correlations, which is fundamental to understanding the boundaries of quantum theory.
